title: GE HealthCare appoints William Grogan as Chief Financial Officer
summary: GE HealthCare appoints William Grogan as Chief Financial Officer
body_text: CHICAGO — August 18, 2026 — GE HealthCare (Nasdaq: GEHC), a leading global precision care innovator, today announced the appointment of William (Bill) Grogan as Chief Financial Officer, effective September 14, 2026. Grogan succeeds Jay Saccaro, who, as previously announced, stepped down for an expanded role outside of the medical technology industry. George Newcomb, who is serving as interim Chief Financial Officer, will continue in his role as Controller and Chief Accounting Officer. Grogan joins GE HealthCare from Xylem Inc., a leading global water solutions company with approximately $9 billion in revenue, where he has served as executive vice president and chief financial officer since 2023. At Xylem, he partnered with the leadership team to execute a strategy to outpace market growth, significantly expanded margins, and simplified operations to fund investment in innovation and higher-growth digital and services offerings. Under his financial leadership, Xylem successfully integrated a $7.5 billion acquisition, delivering cost synergies well ahead of schedule, drove portfolio optimization, and strengthened capital deployment across the business. Prior to Xylem, Grogan spent more than a decade at IDEX Corporation, a diversified global engineered products company delivering mission-critical solutions, including serving as senior vice president and chief financial officer from 2017 to 2023. As CFO, he helped reposition IDEX’s portfolio toward higher-growth markets, a strategy that supported a more than doubling of the company’s market capitalization, while delivering consistent margin expansion and disciplined capital deployment. Earlier in his career, Grogan held finance leadership positions at Walgreens, Crane Co., and Sears Holdings Corp. "I am excited that Bill will serve as our CFO and help lead our next chapter of growth," said Peter Arduini, President and CEO, GE HealthCare. "He combines strong financial leadership with an operator's mindset, grounded in lean business systems and a clear focus on execution. Bill's capabilities will augment our strong leadership team as we advance our precision care strategy and create long-term value for our colleagues, patients, customers, and shareholders." “GE HealthCare’s purpose of creating a world where healthcare has no limits, its commitment to patients, and the opportunity created by this new wave of innovation drew me to the company,” said Grogan. “I am excited to partner with Peter and the leadership team, spend time with our customers, and lead a finance organization that helps turn innovation into profitable growth and long-term value creation.” Grogan serves on the Board of Directors and Audit Committee of Crane NXT and on the Advisory Council for the Girard School of Business at Merrimack College. He holds a Master of Business Administration from Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management and a bachelor’s degree in finance from Merrimack College. title: Retail Data 101 for New Suppliers: POS, Replenishment, and Scorecards
summary: Master retail data fundamentals. Learn how POS, replenishment, and scorecards form a feedback loop that drives your success with major retailers.
body_text: In this article, learn about: The connection between point-of-sale data, replenishment, and supplier scorecards How to interpret retail performance metrics to identify operational gaps Strategies for using data visibility to prevent deductions and strengthen retailer relationships New suppliers often enter the retail world thinking their relationship with a buyer is defined solely by purchase orders (POs) . While the initial item setup and first shipment are significant milestones, they are only the beginning of a continuous, data-driven conversation. The long-term health of your business can be defined by three connected data streams operating in the background: Point-of-sale (POS) data that shows what is actually selling Replenishment data that determines what gets ordered next Scorecards that measure how well you executed against those requirements Instead of viewing these as three separate retailer systems to master, it is more effective to see them as one feedback loop. POS data provides the signal of consumer demand Replenishment is the retailer’s reaction to that signal The scorecard is the final grade on your ability to meet that demand Understanding how these links function allows you to see problems coming before they ever appear as an invoice deduction . Mastering POS Data Every time a customer swipes a card or pays cash at a register, they generate a treasure trove of information. Retail POS data is the cornerstone for understanding not just what shoppers buy, but how they shop and what drives their decisions. POS data summarizes sales totals, as well as encompasses several distinct categories that help you optimize your operations: Sales and basket data: This includes individual transactions, item prices, quantities, and discounts applied. Tracking these trends over time helps you identify peak sales periods, seasonal patterns, and which products might be languishing on the shelf. Inventory and stock levels: This data provides real-time visibility into retail stock levels, including quantities on hand and reorder points. It is the backbone of the supply chain, helping you manage production schedules and reduce the risk of stockouts. Location and time data: By viewing purchases by region, city, or even individual store, you can understand regional variations in consumer preferences. Timestamps also allow you to identify peak hours so that you can plan staffing or promotions accordingly. When brands effectively collect and analyze POS data, they can move away from guesswork and toward data-driven decisions regarding pricing strategies, marketing campaigns, and product assortment. For example, a sudden spike in POS data at a specific store cluster could be an early warning that the current replenishment plan may not be able to meet demand. Related Reading : Point of Sale Data Sharing Understanding Replenishment In supply chain management, replenishment is the movement of inventory from the supplier to the retailer in order to maintain appropriate stock levels. This cycle typically involves moving product from a supplier’s warehouse to a retailer’s distribution center (DC) and finally to the individual store shelves. The standard replenishment cycle follows a typical path: The retailer system identifies a replenishment need based on inventory levels Then the system aggregates those quantities at the DC level Finally, it generates a PO for the supplier The PO includes critical details like the item, quantity, destination, and the Must Arrive by Date (MABD). Most major retailers use one of four broad replenishment processes: Reorder point process: This automated system monitors inventory in real-time. When stock falls below a set minimum threshold, it triggers a reorder. Periodic process: Inventory is checked at set intervals and orders are only placed if stock is low during that check. Seasonal replenishment: This strategy is used for high-demand products sold during specific periods. Stocking occurs during the downtime to prepare for the peak season. Demand replenishment: Stock is only replenished based on actual consumer demand, which reduces overstock; however, it also requires frequent monitoring to avoid stockouts. Successful suppliers should maintain constant vigilance over their demand plans . If you notice your POS sales are trending up, recommending a forecast adjustment can mitigate the risk of future out-of-stocks. Walmart , for instance, accepts some forecast variance dependent on vendor agreements, but consistent misses can lead to poor in-stock rates and strained relationships. Related Reading : What is CPFR? Collaborative Planning, Forecasting, and Replenishment Navigating the Scorecard The scorecard is where the threads of POS and replenishment data converge into a single report on your operational reliability. Retailers use these tools to monitor their suppliers systematically, often using the data to determine shelf placement and reorder volume without ever having a direct conversation with the brand. Using Walmart’s supplier performance scorecard as a primary example, performance is typically broken down into distinct modules: On time in full (OTIF) : OTIF measures if you delivered exactly what was ordered within the required window. For Walmart, the standard targets are 90% on-time for prepaid shipments, 98% for collect ready, and 95% in-full. Supplier quality excellence program (SQEP) : This module measures compliance with packaging, labeling, and shipping accuracy. A high SQEP score indicates your products arrive floor-ready, while a low score points to friction that costs the retailer time and labor. Advance ship notice (ASN) accuracy: This tracks how accurately you transmit shipment data through EDI 856. The ASN must be sent before the truck arrives and must perfectly match the physical shipment. Claims and returns: This module shows what happens after delivery, such as returns due to damage or defects. Each claim represents lost revenue and often signals a process failure upstream. A scorecard defect is usually a symptom of an underlying issue. For example, if your OTIF score is low because of short shipments, the root cause might be a forecasting gap where you did not produce enough to meet the demand spike seen in your POS data weeks earlier. From Symptom to Root Cause The most successful suppliers are those who can trace a scorecard hit back through the feedback loop to find the actual cause. Tracing these patterns requires looking beyond individual defects to see where they cluster. If a specific SKU consistently triggers SQEP fines for labeling, you might have a printer calibration issue or a 3PL packing station error. If you find yourself in the at-risk category on your scorecard, the buyer is likely already managing around your limitations by shrinking order sizes or passing you over for promotional opportunities. Many suppliers in this position have no idea they are underperforming until their orders start getting smaller. The way to stay ahead is to run your own internal scorecard before your next line review. Pull your own data on fill rates, EDI acknowledgment speeds, and ASN timing. If your team is manually managing EDI files or re-entering order data, you are introducing possible failure points that will eventually show up as scorecard defects. Automating these failure-prone steps is the hallmark of a high-performing supplier. Ultimately, mastering these data streams is both efficient and puts suppliers in a competitive position. A supplier who understands how POS data drives replenishment and how execution drives the scorecard can catch problems early, protecting their margins and their shelf space. title: Claude connectors: How to connect Claude to other apps
summary: Here's everything you need to know about Claude connectors: what they are, how to use them, and how to add custom Claude connectors, so you can take action straight from Claude.
body_text: Claude is generally considered to be the best chatbot for almost everything: marketers will tell you it writes better than other chatbots; developers will tell you it codes better; and people who inexplicably think it's a good idea to use AI as a therapist will tell you it's kinder than other models. It's all grounded in reality: Claude is particularly good at reasoning through hard problems, creating original content, and surfacing insights from whatever you throw at it. But if you're using it at work, you also want Claude to actually take action in your other apps, doing things like pulling in your data, creating records, and sending messages. There are a few ways to connect Claude to your other tools. If you've already poked around and gotten confused by the terms—connectors, plugins, MCP—you're in good company (hi). Anthropic has rolled these features out in waves, and the naming hasn't always been intuitive. But after spending more time than I'd like to admit clicking through the docs and settings, here's everything you need to know. Table of contents: What are Claude connectors? What can you do with Claude connectors? How to use Claude connectors How to add Claude custom connectors (MCP servers) Connect Claude to your entire tech stack with Zapier Claude connectors FAQ What are Claude connectors? A Claude connector is a native integration that gives Claude access to an external service—apps like Google Drive, Slack, and GitHub. Connectors handle the authentication and expose the operations Claude can use: searching your files, retrieving content, and doing things inside those apps. In practice, that means you can take action in other apps directly from your Claude chat. Claude connectors vs. Claude plugins Claude connectors and Claude plugins are somehow two different things. Here's what they refer to: Claude connectors are the integrations themselves—the individual connections to services like Gmail, Figma, or Notion. You can browse and install them from the Connectors Directory . Connectors are available to all users on all plans (including free—but you can only use one at a time on a free plan). Claude plugins are installable bundles that can include connectors, but also include skills (pre-built commands) and sub-agents. Those things are then all packaged together for a specific workflow or role. Think of a plugin as a ready-to-go setup for, say, a marketing workflow or a finance research task. Plugins are only available on paid plans. You'll also hear MCP come up a lot. MCP (model context protocol) is the open standard (developed initially by Anthropic) that's working under the hood for these connectors. You don't really need to know the nuances here, though. Focus on figuring out the best way to get Claude connected to the apps you already use. What can you do with Claude connectors? What you can do with a Claude connector depends entirely on what capabilities that connector supports. But generally, you're looking at two categories: Read (search): When Claude has access to your other apps, it can search them and read their contents. That means Claude will have live context for all your questions instead of just relying on its training data or publicly available information. Write (take action): Claude connectors can actually do things in your other apps. That might mean creating issues in a task management app, drafting and sending messages in a chat app, updating records in your CRM, adding files to storage, or whatever the connector supports. An example of what this might look like in practice: a project manager could ask Claude to pull all open issues from Linear, cross-reference them with notes from recent standups in Google Drive, and send a status report to stakeholders in Slack—all without leaving the chat window. How to use Claude connectors Here's how to use connectors in Claude: Click the plus ( + ) button next to the chat window, and select Add connector. The directory will open. Filter based on what you need, or search for the service you want to connect. Click the connector you want, review its description and capabilities, then click Connect. Follow the authentication prompts to grant Claude access to your account. It might open a new browser tab, and some apps offer a quickstart prompt for after installation. Click Allow to give Claude permission to access your account. You'll be brought back to the Claude chat window. Now, you can click the plus sign ( + ) in any conversation, hover over Connectors, and toggle the connector on (though it should be on by default). Claude will also suggest connected apps on its own when they're relevant to what you're asking—you don't have to invoke them explicitly every time. Note: On Team and Enterprise plans, an account owner needs to enable each connector at the org level (then individuals will authenticate on their own). Enterprise plans also support org-managed auth, which lets you authorize a connector once for the entire organization. How to remove connectors from Claude You can remove a Claude connector in a couple ways, but the easiest way is from your settings. Click Customize in the sidebar, and then select Connectors. Find the connector you want to remove, and click it. Click Disconnect . Click Disconnect again in the confirmation modal. If you change your mind, you can always reconnect it. Also, if you just want to turn a connector off for a short time, you can use the toggle method I described earlier. How to add Claude custom connectors (MCP servers) If Claude doesn't natively connect to the app you need it to, or if you've built your own MCP server, you can add it as custom connector. Note : What I'm about to show you is only possible on a personal plans. If you're on a Team or Enterprise plan, your admin will need to enable the custom connector for your entire organization , at which point, you'll be able to find it under Customize > Connectors. Click Customize in the sidebar, and select Connectors . Click Add, and select Add custom connector. Enter the connector's name and the URL of the MCP server. Follow the authentication prompts to grant Claude access to your account. It might open a new browser tab, and some apps offer a quickstart prompt for after installation. Allow any permissions as needed, and click Allow. You'll be brought back to the Claude chat window. When you click the plus sign ( + ) in any conversation and hover over Connectors, you can toggle the connector on (though it should be on by default). But just like with native connectors, Claude should be able to figure out when to use the custom connector without you explicitly telling it. Connect Claude to your entire tech stack with Zapier If you want to connect Claude to your entire tech stack, Zapier is what you're looking for. Zapier has been securely connecting apps for 15 years, and now it lets you build Claude-powered automations or take action directly from Claude in 9,000+ apps. Build deterministic automations and add AI only when you need it Zapier's automation platform lets you build workflows that run in the background. The baseline model is trigger → action: when something happens in one app, Zapier automatically does something else in another app as a result. But you can also add things like filters, formatters, delays, error handling, and conditional paths, and build complex, multi-step workflows connecting your entire tech stack. Then, wherever those workflows need the reasoning or generative power of Claude, you can use AI by Zapier to add Claude steps to the automation—while the rest of the workflow runs without burning unnecessary tokens . You can choose from a variety of Claude models (costing Zapier tasks, not tokens), or bring your own API key. With AI by Zapier, you get something native Claude connectors can't give you at all: the ability to blend AI into deterministic automation . You're not triggering a full AI conversation when you just need a row added to a table. Instead, you have a workflow that uses Claude only where it adds value—and runs automatically everywhere else. Try Zapier Take action directly from Claude with Zapier MCP Zapier MCP is a custom Claude connector that gives you governed access to 9,000+ apps directly from your Claude chat window. Install it once, give it access to the apps and actions you want Claude to work with, and then you can connect to your entire tech stack straight from your chat window. Some examples of what this looks like in practice: Pull your Salesforce pipeline data, calculate a weighted forecast, and push the summary to Google Sheets and Slack—without leaving Claude. Ask Claude to catch you up on what happened in Slack while you were out of office, surface action items, and draft replies. Anything that needs a human touch can get pushed to your to-do list. Pull meeting transcripts and call notes, draft a polished summary with decisions and next steps, and have it ready to send to clients. It works no matter what your team's tech stack looks like, and because you can specify exactly which apps are in scope and which actions are allowed, you're not handing over the keys to your entire stack. And that governance stays in place even if you switch from Claude to another agent harness . If someone on your team wants to use ChatGPT, Gemini, or whatever AI assistant makes sense next quarter, Zapier MCP works across all of them. Try Zapier MCP Claude connectors FAQ Here are some answers to the questions people (rightfully) tend to be asking the most about Claude connectors. Are Claude connectors safe? Yes. Native connectors use OAuth, which means Claude gets scoped access to a service—it can only do what you've authorized, it can't access content you don't have permission to see, and you control what the connector can do. Remember, though, that custom connectors let you connect Claude to any service that hasn't been verified by Anthropic, so you should only connect to servers from sources you trust, and review the authentication permissions carefully. If you use Zapier MCP with Claude, you get that same OAuth-managed, governed authentication across 9,000+ apps. Are Claude connectors free? Connectors are available on all Claude plans, including free (free users are limited to one connector at a time). Plugins—the bundled packages that can include connectors, skills, and sub-agents—are available on paid plans only. How many connectors does Claude have? Anthropic's native Connectors Directory includes 1,200+ services, with more being added regularly. For anything outside that set, you can add a custom connector via MCP, or use Zapier, which covers 9,000+ apps through a single connection. What data can Claude access through connectors? It depends on the connector, but the important part here is that Claude can only access what you can access. For example, if you don't have edit permissions on a Google Sheet, Claude can't bypass that restriction. Related reading: What is Zapier MCP? body_text: A couple of weeks ago, we reported on the market winners and losers from Ford in the latest Hagerty Price Guide update. This week, we’re talking about cross-town rival Chevy. The gainers haven’t gained as much, and the losers haven’t lost as much, so there’s that. Notable absences from this list include first-gen C/K pickups, which are up nearly 4% since April, while second-gen Chevelles are up nearly 3%. Third-gen Camaros, too, are up by a couple of percentage points. The following six cars, however, represent the biggest increases and decreases among classic Chevys, averaged for all body styles and trims for a given model in #2 (excellent) condition. 1983–88 Monte Carlo SS: +15% Mecum Chevy’s Monte Carlo spanned six generations over more than three decades of production. Conceived on the A-body platform for 1970 as a personal luxury car to compete with the likes of the Thunderbird and Grand Prix, by 1978, the third-generation car was radically downsized in keeping with a philosophy of shrinkage across the divisions of General Motors. A sleeker fourth-gen Monte debuted in 1981, and though it was similar to the car it replaced, a convoluted name change meant its chassis was re-named into the now famous G-body moniker in 1982. Following a 12-year hiatus, the Super Sport moniker returned to the Monte Carlo for 1983. The cars were initially offered in white or dark blue, and the SS package included a rear spoiler and revised front fascia, Chevy’s F41 heavy-duty suspension, special wheels with Goodyear Eagle GT tires, and the 305-cubic-inch high-output L69 V-8 cribbed from the Camaro, which put 175 horsepower to the rear wheels through a Turbo 350 automatic. NASCAR success beginning in 1984 helped bolster sales, a better (TH-200 4R) automatic found its way in, and more colors joined the spec sheet, as did the Aerocoupe, starting in 1986. Values for the Monte Carlo SS have been a bit up and down over the last five years, though an uptick in the latest Hagerty Price Guide update has #2-condition examples up to roughly $31,000 , from their springtime pricing of $26,700. In the same period, Aerocoupes have climbed from $29K to $33,400. 1962–67 Chevy II Nova: +11% GM GM introduced the Chevy II in 1962 as a counter to Ford’s incredibly popular Falcon. Small in stature and powered by four- and six-cylinder engines, the compact car was as economical as Chevy machinery got in those days, with a top trim level called the Nova 400. Body styles included two-door sport coupes, four-door sedans, convertibles, and station wagons. By 1964, a 283 V-8 was available, and a 327 joined the lineup a year later, making the Nova SS a force to be reckoned with in straight-line performance. A redesign for 1966 sharpened the Nova’s soft contours, and new engines joined the fray, including a 350-hp L79 V-8. The beauty of the Chevy II Nova was its versatility; from mild people movers to wild muscle machines, there really was (and is) a model for everyone. Naturally, the performance-oriented ’65 Super Sport sits at the top of the range, with #2 examples up from about $24K to nearly $27K in the latest HPG update, and the ’67 SS car with the L30 327 moving from $40,400 to nearly $45,000. A ’64 four-door sedan, meanwhile, gained about $1500 in value in the same period, up from $12,500 to nearly $14,000 today. 1946–48 Stylemaster: +4.4% Mecum As American industry recovered from the enormous contributions required for the war effort, Chevrolet returned to its prewar tooling to get “new” cars out the door. The Stylemaster series was the carmaker’s budget offering and was based on the Master Deluxe of the early 1940s. Compared with the “upscale” Fleetline and mid-tier Fleetmaster, the poverty-spec Stylemaster lacked chrome trim around the windows (the Fleetline also featured chrome strips on the lower half of the fenders and rear quarters. Inside, it featured a more spartan interior and lacked amenities such as a clock, ashtray, and armrests. Power came from a 216.5-cubic-inch inline-six mated to a three-speed column shifter, and body styles included two-door business and club coupes, a two-door town sedan, and a four-door sport sedan. The sedans have been the movers in this group, with values for four-doors climbing from $19,500 to $21,500 and those for two-door sedans jumping from $23,000 to $25,300. 1973–91 Suburban: -9.0% GM Chevrolet introduced the Suburban in 1935, and no other nameplate has enjoyed that kind of production span—now standing at a staggering 91 years over 12 generations. And one of the longest-running generations was the seventh, which hit the streets in 1973. The truck was distinguished from its predecessor not just because of its sharper “square-body” lines, but because it was the first to feature four passenger doors instead of the sixth-gen’s three or the two doors of all previous models. While still infused with the rugged underpinnings that were its bread and butter, the Suburban was also available with more luxury amenities than any before, including A/C, power seats and windows, and less bare-bones upholstery. Two- and four-wheel-drive models were offered (as C and K series, respectively) in both half-ton (C10/K10) and three-quarter ton (C20/K20) payloads. Trims included Custom Deluxe, Scottsdale, and Silverado, and power came from a range of small-block and big-block V-8s, as well as a straight-six for the model’s first six years of production. These were always simple, hardy vehicles, and with so many built over so long a time span, many are still on the road happily chugging away. Since the spring, almost universally, all Suburbans of this generation in excellent shape are down about 9% , so if you’re in the market, their dip in pricing should save you some money. An ’85 C10 Silverado is now a $23K rig, down from $25,400, while a K20 Silverado from the same year is down from just over $31K to just over $28K. Find the trim, powertrain, and layout that works for you, and get after it. 1991–96 Caprice Classic: -5.0% Chevrolet Perhaps no car in Chevy’s catalog ever received a glow-up quite like the fourth-generation Caprice, which went from the exemplary definition of “three-box sedan” to “jellybean” in the blink of an eye. Underneath, however, the aerodynamic new Caprice relied heavily on its predecessor’s B-body platform and powertrains, which included a 4.3-liter V-6 and 5.0-liter V-8, as well as the 5.7-liter V-8 originally meant for 9C1 police versions of the Caprice and, for 1994–96, a detuned, 260-hp LT1 borrowed from the Corvette. The Caprice came in both sedan and wagon form, and a base ’91 Caprice four-door is down about $600 from the spring, to $12,400. A “hot” Caprice Classic LS with the LT1, meanwhile, is down from $23,700 to $22,500. 1975–76 Vega Cosworth: -4.8% Chevrolet It’s a shame the little Vega never made more of a splash than it did. In period, it was arguably a far more attractive alternative to its domestic and import competition. Even today—if you find one in the wild—the shape has aged well. That it was rushed to market was the Vega’s undoing, however, and it was let down by a host of issues, including the reliability of its aluminum four-cylinder engines, despite hundreds of engineering corrections over the car’s production life. Vegas were offered as a hatchback, notchback coupe, two-door wagon, and sedan delivery, but the model people seem to remember most is the hotted-up Vega Cosworth of 1975–76. Development had begun under the direction of John DeLorean, with British engine specialist Cosworth tasked with building a performance engine capable of slaying the little BMWs and Alfas of the day. In the end, the twin-cam all-aluminum 2-liter four was rated at 110 hp, and little more than 3500 were built, with an MSRP of more than $5900—twice the cost of a regular Vega. Vega Cosworths enjoyed a long, steady climb in values beginning in 2016, which accelerated in the pandemic era, before falling off in the last couple of years. Since July 2023, they’re down almost $9000, and the most recent decline has seen excellent ones drop from $22,900 to $21,800. Who can say where the floor is, but if you’ve been looking at these interesting compact performance cars, now might be the time. title: Celebrity Gaming Setups: The PCs That Keep the Spotlight Running
summary: See what specs power celebrity-style gaming and streaming, plus the best prebuilt PCs for balanced performance, multitasking, and value.
body_text: Celebrity gaming is no longer a novelty. It has become a real part of the entertainment mix, where a quick stream, a surprise appearance, or a few competitive matches can pull in a huge audience. Fans tune in for the personality, but they also notice the setup behind the scenes. That is what makes this trend so relevant for shoppers. The same things that help a celebrity look polished on camera also matter to everyday PC buyers: fast load times, smooth gameplay, dependable streaming, and enough system memory to keep everything running without hiccups. In other words, the hardware is part of the experience. If you have ever wondered what kind of gaming PC fits this style of play, the answer usually comes down to balance. A strong CPU, a current-generation GPU, fast storage, and enough RAM to handle gaming plus multitasking. Celebrity gamer culture puts those priorities in the spotlight, but they are the same priorities many buyers already want in a prebuilt desktop. How Celebrity Gamers Became Cultural Power Players Celebrity gaming grew because it feels more personal than a standard promo. Instead of a polished ad, audiences get a live reaction, a funny loss, a clutch win, or a chaotic charity stream. That kind of real-time content gives fans a better sense of the person behind the name, and it makes gaming feel more accessible at the same time. Streaming platforms and short-form clips helped turn these moments into shareable events. One stream can create thousands of highlights, and those clips can travel far beyond the original audience. That is a big reason gaming has become such a strong part of celebrity culture: it is easy to watch, easy to share, and easy to talk about. For the gaming industry, that visibility matters. A celebrity playing a title can bring fresh attention to the game, push it into conversation, and make it feel more mainstream overnight. It can also change how people think about the hardware itself. Once audiences see a setup in action, they start asking practical questions about CPU, GPU, memory, and storage. That shift is useful for shoppers. When performance is visible, so are the specs behind it. If a stream is smooth and the game loads quickly, viewers notice. If the system struggles, they notice that too. Who Needs This Culture, and Why It Matters Celebrity gamer culture is not just for people who follow entertainment news. It affects the way a lot of buyers think about PC shopping. Casual players see gaming as more social and more approachable. Competitive players see the appeal of speed and responsiveness. Families and shared households see how one desktop can cover gaming, schoolwork, streaming, and everyday browsing. That makes the hardware conversation much more practical. Most buyers do not need a flashy showpiece. They want a desktop that powers on quickly, handles modern games without drama, and is ready to use out of the box. That is one reason prebuilt gaming PCs continue to be so popular, especially when they come with Windows 11 already installed. One strong example is the ABS Cyclone Aqua Prebuilt Gaming PC – Windows 11 – Intel Core i5-14400F – GeForce RTX 5060 8GB – DLSS 4 – 32GB DDR4 3200 – 1TB M.2 NVMe SSD . It combines an Intel Core i5-14400F 10-core processor, a ZOTAC GAMING GeForce RTX 5060 Twin Edge OC 8GB GDDR7, 32GB of DDR4-3200 memory, and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD. That spec set is appealing because it is straightforward: enough power for modern games, plenty of memory for multitasking, and storage that keeps things moving. For buyers who want a setup that also works well for streaming or content creation, that balance becomes even more important. The celebrity gaming world may look glamorous, but the real lesson is simple: a good PC should make gaming easier, not more complicated. Real Use-Case Scenarios: From Casual Streams to Competitive Play Not every gamer needs the same kind of PC, and celebrity setups are a good reminder of that. Some people just want to jump into a game and stream casually. Others need extra processing power for live overlays, chat, recording software, and background apps. A few want the best graphics hardware they can justify for a more premium gaming experience. For a casual streamer or multitasker, the ABS Cyclone Aqua with the Core i5-14400F is a very practical fit. Its 32GB DDR4-3200 memory gives you room for browser tabs, voice chat, and recording tools while the game is running. The Kingston SNV3S 1TB PCIe 4.0 x4 NVMe SSD keeps load times quick, and the RTX 5060 8GB GDDR7 supports DLSS 4 in compatible games. That is exactly the kind of setup that fits modern creator-style gaming without overcomplicating the purchase. If you want more breathing room for heavier multitasking, the ABS Cyclone Aqua Prebuilt Gaming PC – Windows 11 – Intel Core i7-14700F – GeForce RTX 5060 8GB – DLSS 4 – 32GB DDR5 – 1TB NVMe SSD is the step-up option. It uses a 20-core Intel Core i7-14700F and 32GB of DDR5-6000 memory, which gives it more room for streaming tools, editing, and background apps. Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.2 also make it a cleaner fit for a wireless desk setup. For shoppers who want to prioritize graphics hardware, the Andromeda Insights AMD Spectra Gaming PC – RX 9070 XT 16GB | Ryzen 5 9600X | 16GB DDR5 6000MHz | 1TB Gen4 SSD | 850W Gold | ARGB | Wi-Fi + BT | Win 11 takes a different route. With an AMD Ryzen 5 9600X, an AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT 16GB, 16GB DDR5-6000 memory, and an 850W 80+ Gold power supply, it is a strong choice for users who want a newer AM5 platform and a more graphics-forward build. And if you are looking for something practical and more affordable, the ABS Flux II Aqua Gaming PC – Windows 11 – Intel Core i5-14400F – GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 8GB – DLSS 4 – 16GB DDR4 3200 – 1TB M.2 SSD keeps the formula simple with a 650W 80 PLUS Gold PSU, Wi-Fi 6, and a 1TB SSD. It is a good reminder that you do not need a top-shelf build to stay current. Best Pick per Scenario If you want to shop like a smart gamer instead of chasing hype, the right choice depends on how you plan to use the PC. Some buyers want the best all-around balance. Others care more about multitasking. A third group wants the strongest GPU they can fit into their budget. Best overall balance: ABS Cyclone Aqua with Intel Core i5-14400F, RTX 5060 8GB GDDR7, and 32GB DDR4-3200. It is the most well-rounded option for gaming, streaming, and daily use. Best for heavier multitasking: ABS Cyclone Aqua with Intel Core i7-14700F and 32GB DDR5-6000. The 20-core CPU and faster memory make it the most flexible choice for content creation and live streaming. Best graphics-first option: Andromeda Insights AMD Spectra with Radeon RX 9070 XT 16GB and Ryzen 5 9600X. It is the strongest pick here for buyers who want a more powerful GPU and a newer AMD platform. Best value-style mainstream build: ABS Flux II Aqua with RTX 5060 Ti 8GB and 16GB DDR4-3200. It keeps the system approachable while still delivering current-gen features like DLSS 4 support. There is also an important platform difference to keep in mind. The DDR4-based ABS systems are appealing if you want a proven, cost-conscious configuration. The DDR5 systems, including the Core i7-14700F build and the Ryzen 5 9600X build, lean more toward buyers who want more bandwidth and a newer foundation. Celebrity gamer culture has made these kinds of specs easier to understand. Viewers are not only watching the person on screen anymore; they are also noticing the machine making the stream possible. That has helped bring CPU cores, memory speed, storage type, and GPU capacity into everyday gaming conversations. The Bigger Impact on the Gaming Community The bigger story here is not celebrity status. It is how gaming has become part of mainstream culture in a way that feels interactive and easy to share. More people are exposed to gaming through familiar faces, and that makes the hobby feel less niche and more approachable. It also helps buyers better understand what matters in a PC. A 32GB dual-channel configuration makes multitasking more comfortable. A 1TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD helps keep load times snappy. A well-chosen GPU can change the whole experience, especially when you want smooth gameplay and reliable streaming at the same time. That is why the hardware behind the stream matters so much. A desktop like the ABS Cyclone Aqua with the Core i5-14400F and RTX 5060 is not just another prebuilt option. It is the kind of machine that fits the way people really use their PCs today: fast to set up, stable under load, and ready for gaming, streaming, and everyday tasks. Celebrity gamer culture is not going away anytime soon because it matches how people consume content now. It is personal, interactive, and built for sharing. The best part is that the same lessons apply to regular PC buyers: focus on balance, choose the right specs for your use case, and pick a system that performs when it matters. Verdict: If you want a gaming PC that captures the practical side of celebrity-style streaming, choose a balanced prebuilt with a modern GPU, at least 32GB of memory, and fast NVMe storage. If you want more room for creator tasks, step up to a stronger CPU and DDR5. If you want the most graphics-focused setup, prioritize the higher-end GPU. The spotlight may be on the streamer, but the right PC keeps the whole show running. Frequently Asked Questions What kind of PC is best for gaming and streaming like a creator? A balanced prebuilt with a modern CPU, a current-gen GPU, fast NVMe storage, and at least 32GB of RAM is usually the best fit. That combination makes it easier to game, stream, keep chat open, and run recording or overlay software at the same time. Do I really need 32GB of RAM for a gaming PC? Not for every game, but 32GB is a smart choice if you plan to stream, edit clips, or multitask while playing. It gives you more headroom so your system stays responsive when multiple apps are open. Is DDR5 worth it over DDR4 in a prebuilt desktop? DDR5 is the better forward-looking option if you want a newer platform and more bandwidth for heavier multitasking. DDR4 is still a strong value choice if you want solid gaming performance and a lower total cost. What is the difference between the RTX 5060 and RTX 5060 Ti for buyers? Both are mainstream GPUs built for modern gaming and streaming features, but the RTX 5060 Ti generally offers more performance headroom. If your priority is value, the RTX 5060 is often enough; if you want extra flexibility for future games, the Ti model is the safer pick. What should I check before buying a prebuilt gaming PC? Start with the CPU, GPU, RAM, storage size, and power supply, since those have the biggest impact on real-world performance. It is also worth checking warranty coverage, wireless features, and whether the system is actually in stock before you buy. title: Harvard Bioscience Announces Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Harvard Bioscience, Inc.'s business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: Second Quarter 2026 Revenue Growth of 11% Year Over Year to $22.7 Million Raises Full Year 2026 Revenue Guidance to 3%-5% Year Over Year Growth HOLLISTON, Mass., Aug. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Harvard Bioscience, Inc. (Nasdaq: HBIO) (the “Company” or “Harvard Bioscience”) today announced financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. "We delivered a strong quarter anchored by 11% top-line growth, reflective of stronger demand and an improved environment across our key customer channels,” said John Duke, President and Chief Executive Officer. “We are seeing solid commercial traction across our telemetry and cellular and molecular technology (CMT) products, driven by our AAA and electroporation businesses, and strong engagement from researchers utilizing our preclinical platform. Outperformance in our CMT products and China drove a slight mix impact on adjusted gross margin. This strong sales momentum positions us to raise our full-year revenue outlook while maintaining our adjusted EBITDA target, supported by ongoing cost discipline and operational progress.” Second Quarter 2026 Results For the second quarter of 2026, the Company reported revenues of $22.7 million compared to $20.5 million in the second quarter of 2025. Revenue for the second quarter of 2026 included a favorable impact from foreign currency exchange rates of approximately 1%, using a constant currency basis. Gross profit for the second quarter of 2026 was $12.6 million compared to $11.5 million in the second quarter of 2025. Gross margin for the second quarter of 2026 was 55.6%, compared to 56.4% in the second quarter of 2025. Adjusted gross profit and adjusted gross margin for the second quarter of 2026 was $12.9 million and 56.7%, respectively, compared with $11.7 million and 57.2% in the same period of the prior year. Net loss for the second quarter of 2026 was ($2.9) million, compared to a net loss of ($2.3) million in the second quarter of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA for the second quarter of 2026 was $1.7 million compared to $1.5 million in the second quarter of the prior year. Six Months Ended June 30, 2026 Results For the six months ended June 30, 2026, the Company reported revenues of $43.5 million, compared to $42.2 million in the same period of the prior year. Revenue for the six months ended June 30, 2026, included a favorable impact from foreign currency exchange rates of approximately 2%, using a constant currency basis. Gross profit was $24.9 million for the first six months of 2026 compared to $23.7 million in the same period of the prior year. Gross margin for the six months ended June 30, 2026, was 57.2% compared with 56.2% in the same period of the prior year. Adjusted gross profit and adjusted gross margin for the six months ended June 30, 2026, was $25.3 million and 58.3%, respectively, compared with $24.1 million and 57.0% in the same period of the prior year. Net loss for the six months ended June 30, 2026, was ($6.3) million compared to a net loss of ($52.6) million in the same period of the prior year, primarily due to goodwill impairment in the first quarter of 2025 of $48.0 million. Adjusted EBITDA for the six months ended June 30, 2026, was $2.4 million, compared to adjusted EBITDA of $2.3 million for the same period of the prior year. Cash (used in) provided by operations was ($0.3) million during the six months ended June 30, 2026 compared to $5.7 million in the same period of the prior year. This press release includes certain financial information presented on an adjusted, or non-GAAP, basis. For additional information on the non-GAAP financial measures included in this press release, see “Use of Non-GAAP Financial Information” and “Reconciliation of GAAP to Non-GAAP Financial Measures” below. Third Quarter 2026 Guidance The Company’s third quarter outlook reflects expected mid-single-digit year-over-year revenue growth at the midpoint of guidance, driven by expected ongoing demand across CMT and new product innovation (NPI) platforms and improving year-over-year profitability on an adjusted EBITDA basis. The Company expects: Revenue between $21.0 million and $22.6 million Adjusted gross margin between 56% and 58% Adjusted EBITDA between $1.5 million and $2.5 million Full Year 2026 Guidance The Company is raising its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to reflect expected strong CMT portfolio momentum and continued adoption of its NPI pipeline, while updating its full-year adjusted gross margin target to account for expected higher-volume of lower-margin CMT product and geographic mix. The Company now expects: Revenue growth between 3% and 5% Adjusted gross margin between 57% and 59% Adjusted EBITDA growth between 6% and 10% Webcast and Conference Call Details In conjunction with this announcement, Harvard Bioscience will be hosting a conference call and webcast today at 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time. A presentation that will be referenced during the webcast will be posted to the Company’s Investor Relations website shortly before the webcast begins. Analysts who would like to join the call and ask a question must register here . Once registered, you will receive the dial-in numbers and a unique PIN number. Participants who would like to join the audio-only webcast should go to our events and presentations on the investor website here . Use of Non-GAAP Financial Information In this press release we have included non-GAAP financial information, including one or more of adjusted operating income (loss), adjusted operating margin, adjusted gross margin, adjusted net income (loss), adjusted EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA margin, diluted adjusted earnings (loss) per share, net debt, adjusted gross profit, and non-GAAP revenue on a constant currency basis. We believe that this non-GAAP financial information provides investors with an enhanced understanding of the underlying operations of our business. For the periods presented, these non-GAAP financial measures have excluded certain expenses and income resulting from items that we do not believe are reflective of the underlying operations of the business. Items excluded include stock-based compensation, amortization of intangibles related to acquisitions, restructuring charges, other operating expenses, goodwill impairment, interest and other expense, net, income taxes, and the tax impact of reconciling items. Management believes that this non-GAAP financial information is important in comparing current results with prior period results and is useful to investors and financial analysts in assessing the Company’s operating performance. Historical non-GAAP financial information included herein is accompanied by a reconciliation to the nearest corresponding GAAP measure, which is included below. In addition, the forward-looking Adjusted gross margin and Adjusted EBITDA guidance for the third quarter of 2026 and full-year 2026 excludes potential charges or gains that may be recorded during the fiscal year, including among other things, restructuring and reorganization expenses, and non-GAAP restructuring related expenses. The Company has not attempted to provide reconciliations of such forward-looking non-GAAP earnings guidance to the comparable GAAP measure, as permitted by Item 10(e)(1)(i)(B) of Regulation S-K, because the impact and timing of these potential charges or gains is inherently uncertain and difficult to predict and is unavailable without unreasonable efforts. In addition, the Company believes such reconciliations would imply a degree of precision and certainty that could be misleading to investors. Such items could have a substantial impact on GAAP measures of the Company’s financial performance. The non-GAAP financial information provided in this press release should be considered in addition to, not as a substitute for, the financial information provided and presented in accordance with GAAP and may be different from other companies’ non-GAAP financial information. title: What Is an AI Data Warehouse? A Practical Enterprise Guide
summary: An AI data warehouse unifies enterprise data, business context, and governance so teams and AI systems can find, explain, and use trusted information.
body_text: An AI data warehouse is an enterprise data foundation that does more than store tables for reporting. It brings together structured records, documents, metadata, business definitions, permissions, and lineage so people and AI systems can find the right information, understand its meaning, and use it with appropriate controls. The important distinction is not that an AI data warehouse replaces every database, lake, or warehouse. It is that it treats context and governed access as part of the data product , rather than leaving them in disconnected catalogs, prompts, spreadsheets, or tribal knowledge. For a private-equity team, that might mean relating a portfolio company’s monthly reporting package to its legal entities, debt schedule, operating metrics, and source files. For an investment bank, it might mean connecting a company profile, comparable transactions, diligence documents, and internal approvals without asking an analyst to rebuild the context for every question. o11 is building in this direction: an AI data warehouse designed to organize complex enterprise information so it can be used by people and agents. The fit is especially clear in financial services, but the underlying problem exists in any enterprise with fragmented systems, sensitive data, and business questions that cross departmental boundaries. See the o11 AI data warehouse solution for the product context, and the private equity and investment banking pages for examples of the financial-services problem. The short answer: what makes a warehouse “AI” Calling a system an AI data warehouse should imply more than adding a chatbot to a SQL interface. A useful AI data warehouse has at least five layers: Data access. It can connect to the systems and files where the organization actually works, not only a clean database prepared for a demo. A durable data model. It represents entities, relationships, metrics, documents, and events in a way that can be reused across questions. Business context. It records definitions, synonyms, ownership, time periods, and assumptions so “revenue,” “EBITDA,” or “customer” mean something specific. Governance and provenance. It can enforce or inherit permissions and show where an answer came from, including relevant source records and transformations. AI interfaces. It gives search, retrieval, analysis, and agents a reliable way to use the data without treating generated text as a substitute for evidence. These layers are related but not identical. A conventional cloud warehouse can be highly scalable and well governed. A vector database can retrieve semantically similar text. A catalog can describe tables. An AI data warehouse is the attempt to make the whole path—from source to meaning to permitted action—work as one operating system for enterprise data. Why traditional data access breaks under AI workloads Most companies do not have one “data source.” They have an estate. A CRM contains accounts and opportunities. An ERP contains invoices and general-ledger entries. A data room contains contracts, presentations, and diligence files. Email contains decisions that explain why a number changed. Analysts maintain local workbooks because an official model does not contain the exact cut of data required for the meeting tomorrow. The data warehouse is valuable because it creates a governed analytical center. But the center often covers only the subset of information that a team had time and budget to model. Documents remain outside. Definitions live in a wiki. Access policies are implemented separately in each application. A question such as “Which portfolio companies missed the plan because of pricing, and what did management say about the cause?” crosses every boundary at once. AI makes the boundary more visible. A language model can summarize any text put in its context window, but it cannot reliably infer which of three similarly named entities is the right one, whether a document is current, or whether the person asking is allowed to see it. Retrieval improves reach, but retrieval without identity, lineage, and business semantics can produce a plausible answer with the wrong evidence. An AI data warehouse is therefore not only a storage choice. It is a design choice about how an organization makes data understandable and usable under changing questions. The building blocks Sources and ingestion Begin with the real sources: databases, SaaS systems, cloud storage, spreadsheets, PDFs, email exports, and APIs. A useful foundation preserves the original record and records when it was observed. Raw files should not be silently overwritten by a cleaned version. The organization needs to distinguish the source value, a normalized value, and an interpretation generated by a model. Ingestion can be batch, event-driven, or on demand. The right choice depends on the question. A risk dashboard may need frequent updates; a historical diligence archive may be refreshed when a new version arrives. Google’s BigQuery documentation describes both ETL and ELT as valid integration patterns and recommends choosing based on existing processes and the desired division of work, rather than treating one acronym as universally correct. BigQuery data integration guidance Entity and relationship modeling Tables are not enough when the question spans systems. The foundation needs durable identifiers for people, companies, funds, deals, facilities, products, and documents. It also needs relationships: a company belongs to a fund, a facility supports an acquisition, a document describes a period, and a metric is reported by an entity. Entity resolution should be explicit and reviewable. “Acme Holdings,” “Acme Holdco LLC,” and an abbreviated ticker may or may not refer to the same entity. A system can suggest a match, but high-impact workflows should retain the evidence and provide a way for a human to confirm or reject it. Semantic context Business terms are part of the data model. “Bookings,” “billings,” “revenue,” and “ARR” are not interchangeable merely because they appear near one another in a document. A semantic layer can define metrics and relationships, but it should also make room for the source, time basis, currency, and calculation assumptions. Snowflake’s documentation describes semantic views as database objects that define business metrics, entities, and their relationships. That is a useful example of why semantics belongs close to governed data, even when the surrounding architecture uses other tools. Snowflake semantic views and architecture Retrieval and reasoning AI interfaces should select evidence before generating an answer. Hybrid retrieval—combining structured filters, keyword search, semantic similarity, and relationship traversal—is often more appropriate than relying on a single vector search. A question about a deal may need a date filter, an entity join, an exact figure, and a paragraph from a board memo. The answer should carry enough context to be checked. That may be a citation, source file, row-level reference, query, calculation, or a short explanation of how a value was reconciled. The goal is not to make every interaction slow with a forensic report. It is to make important claims inspectable. Security and governance Permissions must travel with the data. If the source system restricts a document to a deal team, a retrieval layer should not expose that document simply because it was indexed elsewhere. Governance also includes retention, deletion, audit logging, model-provider boundaries, and the handling of confidential information. NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary and sector-neutral, but its emphasis on governing, mapping, measuring, and managing risks is a helpful design lens. The NIST generative-AI profile specifically recommends documenting data origin and content lineage, along with upstream dependencies and evaluation methods. NIST AI RMF and NIST Generative AI Profile AI data warehouse versus adjacent systems The phrase can become vague if it is used as a synonym for every modern data product. The following distinctions help. System Primary job What it usually leaves to other layers Operational database Run a business application and transactions Cross-system analytics, enterprise history, broad discovery Data warehouse Store modeled data for analytics and reporting Unmodeled documents, broad context, agent-ready retrieval Data lake Store large volumes of raw or semi-structured data Consistent business semantics and analyst-friendly governance Vector database Retrieve items by semantic similarity Relational truth, permissions, metrics, and lineage Catalog or semantic layer Describe data and business definitions Ingestion, storage, and end-to-end workflows AI data warehouse Connect data, context, governance, and AI access It still depends on source quality, policy decisions, and human review These are not mutually exclusive. A production architecture may use a warehouse for curated facts, a lakehouse for open files, a catalog for discovery, and an AI data warehouse layer to coordinate context and access. The question is which layer owns the user-facing experience and the cross-system model. A practical example: portfolio-company performance Imagine an investment team asks, “Which companies are more than 10% below the latest operating plan, what changed since last month, and what actions did management commit to?” A report-only workflow might query a finance mart for variance, then ask an analyst to open several emails and operating reviews. A document-only workflow might find the right phrases but miss the exact plan version and entity. An AI data warehouse workflow can: identify the portfolio company and reporting period; select the approved plan and current actuals; calculate the variance using a named metric; retrieve the operating review and relevant commitments; show the sources and access checks; draft an answer that a professional can review. The hard part is not producing the prose. It is maintaining the links between data, time, definitions, and evidence as the company changes. What an AI data warehouse does not solve It does not make bad source data correct. It cannot decide a disputed accounting policy without an accountable owner. It does not eliminate the need for data contracts, retention rules, incident response, or domain experts. Nor does it guarantee that an AI answer is accurate simply because the answer includes a citation; the cited source may be stale, ambiguous, or misinterpreted. Teams should also resist the idea that every dataset belongs in one central platform. Some data should remain in an operational system, a regulated environment, or a specialized analytical store. Federation and governed references can be better than copying everything. The right architecture is the one that makes high-value questions reliable at an acceptable cost and risk. How to evaluate one Ask vendors and internal teams to demonstrate a complete path, not a polished chat screen: Connect a representative set of structured and unstructured sources. Resolve duplicate entities and show how uncertain matches are reviewed. Define a metric with its owner, time basis, and calculation. Ask a cross-source question that requires both a number and a document. Test the same question with two identities that have different permissions. Change a source schema or upload a new document version. Inspect the resulting lineage, citations, audit log, and failure behavior. The test should include an intentionally ambiguous question. A system that asks for clarification or says “I do not have enough evidence” may be safer than one that always returns a confident paragraph. A useful mental model Think of the warehouse as a governed map, not a magic answer machine. The map records where data lives, what entities it describes, how records relate, which definitions are approved, and who can use each source. AI can help people navigate that map and carry out work, but the map still needs owners and updates. This framing keeps architecture decisions practical: add the layer that makes the next important question more reliable, and keep deterministic systems where determinism is required. FAQs Is an AI data warehouse the same as a data warehouse with an LLM? No. An LLM interface can make a warehouse easier to query, but an AI data warehouse also needs context, retrieval, permissions, provenance, and workflow controls. The exact boundary varies by product, so evaluate the underlying data model and evidence path. Does an AI data warehouse replace Snowflake, Databricks, or BigQuery? Not necessarily. Those platforms provide mature storage, compute, ingestion, governance, and analytics capabilities. An AI data warehouse may use one of them, complement them, or focus on a different layer: connecting enterprise context and AI access to the data estate. Does it require structured data? No, but structured data remains important. Documents, email, and files need to be related to structured entities and periods if the resulting answers are to be reliable. Treating every source as unstructured text loses useful constraints. Can a small company use one? Yes, if it has cross-system questions and expects its data estate to grow. A small company should begin with a narrow, high-value workflow rather than building an enterprise-wide ontology before it has a clear user need. Is “self-maintaining” automatic? It should mean that the system detects and handles routine changes with limited manual intervention, while surfacing exceptions for review. It should not mean that every schema change, entity match, or business-policy change is accepted without control. Sources and further reading Snowflake key concepts and architecture BigQuery overview BigQuery loading, transforming, and exporting data AWS: What is a data lakehouse? NIST AI Risk Management Framework resources NIST Generative AI Profile The practical definition is simple: an AI data warehouse makes enterprise data usable by AI without discarding the structure, context, and controls that make the data trustworthy in the first place.

Agent Skills: The AI Operating System for Sales Managers
summary: Introducing Agent Skills, configurable, contextualized, permission-aware AI workflows built on Ambition's Performance Graph.
body_text: Ambition's Agent Skills are configurable, contextualized, permission-aware, and built on Ambition's Performance Graph Ambition, the coaching and performance platform for revenue teams, today launched Agent Skills, a library of out-of-the-box, composable AI workflows that turn the rituals of sales management—coaching prep, pipeline inspection, forecast reviews, performance check-ins, and QBR analysis—into AI actions any member of a revenue organization can run. Every revenue organization runs weekly rituals to drive performance, but most managers spend more time on prep than on coaching, and the frequency and quality of coaching varies by manager. Agent Skills automate the analysis behind each operation, so managers can focus on the conversation rather than the spreadsheet. Revenue Operations teams can configure each Skill to match their organization’s methodology—adjusting data inputs, grounding analysis in uploaded documentation through Procedures, and scheduling Skills into recurring workflows—all with permissions that respect each user’s data access. Every Skill computes its answers from Ambition’s Performance Graph, so every figure traces to a query. "When getting value from AI requires writing the perfect prompt, you've quietly limited that value to your most technically savvy people," said Jared Houghton, CEO and Co-founder of Ambition. "Agent Skills put the full power of Ambition's AI a click away for everyone on the team. That includes the exec walking into a business review, the manager heading into a one-on-one, and the rep deciding where to focus today.” See it: Executive visibility without the deck-building For leadership, Ambition delivers organization, team, and group-level briefs on demand, pulling performance, pipeline, coaching health, and recognition into a single view. Skills include: Executive Org Brief : Company-wide performance, pipeline movement, goal health, coaching program signals, and recognition, distilled into the level of detail leadership needs. Weekly Team Recap and Team Performance Snapshot : The same visibility scoped to any team or group, so leaders can zoom in without waiting on a manually compiled report. Scale it: Manager coaching that works at any team size New manager-facing Skills ensure coaching quality holds as teams grow: Coaching Prep : A complete pre-read for every 1:1, built from scorecard performance, goals, metric trends, peer context, and coaching history. Weekly Manager Brief : The key action items a manager should take this week, each tied to a specific person and target. Rep Goal Builder : A measurable, individualized goal for any rep using their recent trend, targets, and peer standing. Skills give managers the same quality of preparation and prioritization whether they oversee eight reps or forty. Self-serve it: Reps see their own numbers, on their own terms Reps get direct, self-serve access to the same data informing their manager’s coaching: My Week Plan : Turns a rep's scorecard, metrics, goals, pipeline, and coaching action items into a single weekly plan. My Performance Review : A data-backed view of how a rep tracks against their targets, trends, and peers. Built in, not bolted on Every Skill generates from data and coaching activity already inside Ambition; no exporting rosters to a separate BI tool or pasting coaching notes into an outside AI assistant. Performance data stays governed, visible, and in context. “Two of the most pressing challenges in sales performance management are inconsistent coaching and Shadow AI,” said Brian Trautschold, COO and Co-founder of Ambition. “CROs face revenue risk and seller attrition from inconsistent management, while forward-thinking managers copy CRM screenshots into LLMs to generate coaching plans—with no organizational visibility or accountability. Agent Skills bring consistency and context to AI across every level of the revenue org.” About Ambition Ambition is the AI-powered coaching and performance platform that helps organizations operationalize coaching, performance management, and execution across revenue teams. By combining seller activation, coaching orchestration, and performance intelligence, Ambition enables companies to drive predictable growth, improve forecast confidence, and scale high-performing revenue cultures. For media inquiries, contact: marketing@ambition.com ‍

title: If You Think You Keep Seeing Henning Kjærnulf’s Razorblade Chairs in Chic Homes, You’re Right
summary: The mid-century Danish model has become a favorite among interior designers.
body_text: In the breakfast nook of a Lake Tahoe family home, Catherine Kwong placed a set of Henning Kjærnulf’s Razorblade chairs that she purchased on 1stDibs. Photo by William Jess Laird Henning Kjærnulf’s Razorblade chair is constructed of contradictions. Its broad oak frame seems weighty, almost primitive, while the pointed cutouts in its crest rail convey an unexpected delicacy. Depending on the angle you view it from, the back might suggest a crown, a row of gothic arches or the object that inspired the model’s namesake: a double-edged razor blade. The chair has lately become a fixture in design-forward interiors, appearing, for instance, in Catherine Kwong’s room for the 2026 1stDibs 50 and pulled up to the breakfast table in designer Molly Kidd’s Oregon home . Complete sets are highly coveted. Kjærnulf is an elusive figure in Danish design history. His career is much less well documented than those of such late-20th-century contemporaries as Hans Wegner , Børge Mogensen and Finn Juhl . “Razorblade” even seems to have been a late nickname for the model rather than an original designation. Offered on 1stDibs by eliaselias , this 1960s oak Henning Kjærnulf Razorblade chair sports a lambswool-upholstered seat. “Where many Danish designers pursued refinement through simplicity, Kjærnulf wasn’t afraid to embrace ornamentation,” says Benjamin Elias, co-owner of the Denmark-based vintage dealer eliaselias , which has sourced and sold numerous Kjærnulf pieces on its 1stDibs storefront. Elias has noticed interest in Kjærnulf grow over the past few years, especially after the pandemic, as consumers shifted their focus to the home-decor sector and collectors began searching beyond established names for furniture with more individuality. “These pieces have elements of brutalism and traditional craftsmanship, while still fitting naturally into contemporary interiors,” says Elias. “Even from across a room, you know it’s a Kjærnulf chair.” Katie Monkhouse chose a set of Razorblade chairs for the dining room of a young family’s San Francisco home. Photo by Stephanie Russo Those qualities make the model particularly useful to designers. Katie Monkhouse , who first encountered Razorblade chairs at the Round Top Antiques Fair, in Texas, almost a decade ago, likes pairing them with a clean-lined table. “I think they have a lot of character and whimsy without feeling kitschy,” Monkhouse says. “The oak’s neutral, medium tone also distinguishes it from the orange cast associated with many mid-century pieces.” In Molly Kidd’s own Oregon home, she placed a pair of Razorblade chairs at a custom reclaimed-wood table, across from a banquette. Photo by Tim Lenz In Molly Kidd’s breakfast nook, the chairs provide a counterpoint to the plaster walls, linen curtains, rounded forms and rustic reclaimed-wood table. “They have these crisp, graphic lines that act almost like punctuation within an otherwise very relaxed composition,” she says. “I wanted something with a sharper silhouette and durability to keep it from feeling overly precious, especially with my kids.” Elias notes that in other contexts, bouclé, shearling or lambswool upholstery can be used to temper the chairs’ hard geometry with a softer, tactile surface. Rising demand has made complete sets increasingly difficult to find. Many dining suites were dispersed, and matching groups of 8 or 10 are now especially scarce. Elias advises buyers seeking original models to examine a potential purchase’s joinery, consistency of craftsmanship and age-appropriate wear, along with manufacturer’s labels or stamps. Set of four 1960s oak Henning Kjærnulf Razorblade dining chairs from H. Gallery For Kidd, her chairs’ value has little to do with their rarity or the current demand for them. Her family uses them daily, allowing the oak and finish to age gracefully, gaining character with each passing year. “These chairs are part of our everyday life,” she says. “We have coffee there every morning, my kids climb on them, and friends linger around the table long after dinner is over. That’s what I love most about these vintage pieces. They become more beautiful because they’re lived with.” Shop Henning Kjærnulf Razorblade Chairs View All

title: Indonesia Energy Corporation Reports Progress on Drilling of K-29 Well
summary: Company Also Announces Presentation at the 31st Annual EnerCom Energy Investment Conference on August 19 JAKARTA, INDONESIA AND DANVILLE, CA, Aug. 13,...
body_text: Company Also Announces Presentation at the 31st Annual EnerCom Energy Investment Conference on August 19 JAKARTA, INDONESIA AND DANVILLE, CA, Aug. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Indonesia Energy Corporation (NYSE American: INDO) ("IEC"), an oil and gas exploration and production company focused on Indonesia, today announced that its K-29 well, which was spudded on July 25, 2026, continues to drill ahead on schedule and has reached a depth of more than 2,500 feet. The planned total depth of the well is approximately 3,400 feet. At approximately 3,000 feet, IEC expects to enter the targeted reservoir zone, after which IEC plans to conduct a coring job in the target zone. This is to determine the optimal stimulation method based on the rock's natural characteristics for maintaining and enhancing the initial production of the well. Drilling will then proceed to the target depth, followed by wireline logging, casing and cementing, and perforation, before the well is finally prepared for production. This final phase is expected to take several additional weeks, and IEC plans to provide an update once all well operations are complete.
